title: Orthodox Pascha
hook: at midnight: Christ is risen! Truly he is risen! and eggs dyed red for his blood

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sunrise service: chairs on wet grass facing east, and Mary hearing her name in the half-light. Your line was early, while it was dark. Did you catch the sky changing? Day one thousand thirty-six.

"Christ is risen!" A priest shouts it at midnight from the doors of a church, and the crowd packed outside shouts back: "Truly he is risen!" He calls it again. They answer again. Over and over, in whatever language the parish prays. A little while ago the church was dark; now every hand holds a lit candle, and the bells are going. Old men shout it. Children shout it louder. When the service is over, people go home to break the long fast, and on the table, in a bowl, are eggs dyed deep red. Today, Orthodox Pascha.

Start with the name. Paul writes, in the King James: "For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us." The Greek word behind passover there is pascha, and it's the word Orthodox Christians use for Easter itself. The feast is the Passover of Christ, from death to life. Now the call and answer. Luke says that on the first Easter evening, when two friends came back to Jerusalem from Emmaus, the disciples met them with: "The Lord is risen indeed." Pascha turns that into a greeting with two voices. One person says it, and someone else has to say it back. The news isn't finished until a second voice agrees. Through the night the choir sings a short hymn again and again: Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death, and giving life to those in the tombs. Trampling down death by death. Not escaping it. Walking through it and breaking it from the inside, the way the icon shows him standing on the broken gates. Then a sermon is read that tradition credits to John Chrysostom. It invites everyone to the feast: those who kept the fast, and those who didn't; those who came early and those who came at the last hour. Let no one fear death, it says. Then the eggs. Tradition says the red is for the blood of Christ, and the shell is the sealed tomb that breaks open. There's a story people tell about Mary Magdalene and an egg that turned red, but it isn't in the Gospels. In some places people tap their eggs together, one saying Christ is risen, the other answering, to see whose cracks.

Here's the practice: dye or decorate an egg. If you have one, hold it and mark it, even with a pen: a cross, a line, a little color. If you don't, hold any small, smooth thing. Settle, and breathe. Feel the shell, closed and still, made to be broken open. If you pray, you can say the old greeting under your breath, both halves: Christ is risen. Truly he is risen. If you don't, simply notice what the egg is like, sealed now, and meant to open. The bell holds the time.
Orthodox Pascha. Easter as Orthodox Christians keep it: a midnight call of Christ is risen, the answer truly he is risen, and red eggs at the end of the fast.

Your line: truly he is risen. This week ran from a bare altar, through the stations and the seven words, the broken gates, the fire and the dawn, to midnight. Today, when someone tells you good news, be the second voice: say it back. Day one thousand thirty-six.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians keep Pascha with a midnight service: the light passed from one candle, the greeting "Christ is risen!" answered "Truly he is risen!", and a meal afterward that breaks the fast, with eggs dyed red. The date can fall on a different Sunday from Western Easter.

fork.setup: it's midnight. the priest turns to the crowd with his candle and calls out, Christ is risen! you're standing among them. what comes back?
fork.reveal: the whole crowd shouts it back, again and again. the news isn't finished until a second voice agrees.

original.note: Greek: truly he is risen — the answer to Χριστὸς ἀνέστη, Christ is risen.

trapdoor: what you thought: Easter, with a Greek name.
what it means: a midnight feast of call and answer, one flame passed through a crowd, and eggs dyed red for his blood.
what a scholar hears: Paul's "Christ our passover" uses the word pascha (1 Corinthians 5:7), and the answer echoes Luke 24:34, "the Lord is risen indeed."

notes: Week end (days 1030–1036): the carry looks back at the week.

The Paschal troparion and the Chrysostom homily are paraphrased, not quoted (English versions vary and public-domain wording was not verified). 'Trampling down death by death' is a common rendering of the troparion; confirm it may stand unquoted.
'The Greek word behind passover there is pascha' (1 Corinthians 5:7) is a claim about the Greek text; confirm. No wider etymology is given.

Claims rule: no count of days the greeting is used; the meaning of red eggs is attributed to tradition, and the Mary Magdalene egg story to 'a story people tell'. Egg-tapping attributed to 'some places'. Confirm with an Orthodox Keeper.
The 'long fast' is unquantified; the date difference is stated as 'can fall on a different Sunday'.
Original: Ἀληθῶς ἀνέστη / Χριστὸς ἀνέστη, modern Greek pronunciation; confirm.
